name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 4 July 1970

clue.text: Loafers, those vagrant hens?

blocks.note: first meaning: idle people who do no work
second meaning, read literally: hens that wander and drop their eggs here and there

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as LAY ABOUTS: hens that lay about the place, wherever they happen to wander.
explanation.definitionFit: A layabout is a habitual idler, exactly what calling someone a loafer implies in everyday speech.

clue.text: Damp home of one allegedly blithe at hail

definitions.text: Damp home of one allegedly blithe at hail

blocks.note: surface reading: a soggy, badly kept house
setter's reading: Shelley hailed the skylark as a 'blithe spirit', and that bird builds on the wet ground

explanation.surface: A cheerful tenant puts up with a soggy house even when the hail comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's poem To a Skylark opens 'Hail to thee, blithe spirit!', so 'blithe at hail' is the songbird; it nests in a scrape on open ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The skylark nests in grass on the open ground, so its nest is a moist dwelling for that cheerful bird.

clue.text: Truly approaching the signing

blocks.note: surface reading: genuinely, honestly
setter's reading: the word that sits just before 'truly' as a letter closes and the writer signs off

explanation.surface: Someone is really, truly getting near to signing a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Letters traditionally end with the formula '... truly' immediately above the signature.
explanation.definitionFit: The conventional letter ending pairs this word with 'truly' right before the writer puts down a name.

clue.text: Bruin no boob, describes misfortunes stoically

definitions.note: the definition is 'stoically', framed as the way misfortunes are borne

blocks.note: Bruin is the traditional name for a bear in fables
not making a blunder, i.e. doing it competently

explanation.surface: A bear that makes no blunder takes its bad luck with a stiff upper lip.
explanation.definitionFit: Misfortunes borne stoically are endured in a tolerable, manageable way rather than with collapse.

clue.text: You cross where you can in Middlesex

definitions.note: the answer is a town in Middlesex

blocks.note: U sounds like 'you', as in text-speak
a cross is the letter-shaped mark X
where you can cross a river, reading 'cross' a second time

explanation.surface: Directions telling you where a crossing point can be found in Middlesex.
explanation.walkthrough: Middlesex was an English county now mostly absorbed into Greater London; this town lies on its western edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Uxbridge is a town in west London that historically belonged to the county of Middlesex.

clue.text: Playwright for an O.U. D.S.R.A. production

indicators.note: a theatre production stages and arranges material afresh, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the six capitals taken as letters; OUDS is the Oxford University Dramatic Society

explanation.surface: A dramatist is chosen for a staging by the Oxford student drama society.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots make it look like a set of initials for a student society; only the letters matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Victorien Sardou was a nineteenth-century French dramatist, author of the play Tosca adapted by Puccini.

clue.text: Given to an aging Mountie?

blocks.note: surface reading: something presented to an elderly Canadian mounted policeman
setter's reading: anyone mounting a horse, who when old needs a boost from cupped hands

explanation.surface: A gift handed to a veteran of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase literally means hoisting a rider into the saddle, and figuratively any helping boost.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff older rider needs a helper to cup hands under the knee and lift them onto the horse.

clue.text: Forced payments for the forces

blocks.note: first meaning: taxes or charges imposed compulsorily
second meaning: bodies of troops raised by conscription

explanation.surface: Compulsory taxes raised to pay for the armed services.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both compulsory taxes collected by authority and soldiers enlisted by compulsion.

clue.text: One of two boat propellers at the helm for a stage

definitions.text: One of two boat propellers at the helm for a stage

blocks.clueFragment: One of two boat propellers at the helm
blocks.note: surface reading: one of a pair of engines or oarsmen steering a vessel
setter's reading: one of the two Venetian boatmen who lead a Gilbert and Sullivan opera on the stage

explanation.surface: A boat with twin drives being steered through one leg of a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers has two heroes, Marco and Giuseppe, who jointly reign; 'stage' looks like a leg of a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: A Venetian boatman propels his craft with a single oar, and two such men star in the Savoy opera.

clue.text: Assure? I've to make absolutely sure

definitions.note: posit means assert or lay down as fact

indicators.note: the clue says the answer needs the other word added to make the longer word, so that piece is taken away from it

blocks.note: certain beyond doubt
taken as written, the piece that is removed

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to give an assurance, needing to be certain first.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as 'the answer with I'VE makes absolutely sure': POSIT plus IVE is POSITIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit something is to put it forward as true, which is close to stating it with assurance.

clue.text: Stalky, red perforce, in a stew

definitions.text: Stalky, red perforce, in a stew

blocks.clueFragment: Stalky, red perforce, in a stew
blocks.note: surface reading: a person, perhaps Kipling's schoolboy Stalky, flushed and agitated
setter's reading: a plant with red stalks that is usually eaten stewed

explanation.surface: Someone called Stalky is necessarily red-faced because they are in a state of agitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalky' looks like a nickname and 'in a stew' like being flustered; the word is also stage slang for background muttering.
explanation.definitionFit: This garden plant has long red stalks that are cooked with sugar, typically stewed as a dessert.

clue.text: Gorgeous subjects for vintage Academy show?

definitions.note: a pun: subjects relating to gorges

blocks.note: RA is the Royal Academy of Arts in London
a vintage is the grape harvest, gathered from these plants

explanation.surface: Beautiful paintings for a classic Royal Academy exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gorgeous' means beautiful in the surface, but is split as gorge-ous: things like gorges.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep narrow valleys cut by water are what a gorge is, so these are gorge-like features of landscape.

clue.text: Shakespeare tells retrospective fools to shut up

definitions.note: an exclamation meaning 'be quiet', not a verb

indicators.note: looking back over its shoulder, so the word is taken from its last letter to its first

blocks.note: asses are foolish people

explanation.surface: The Bard orders some backward-looking idiots to be quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Taming of the Shrew, the drunk Christopher Sly cries 'Sessa!', taken to mean 'be quiet' or 'let it go'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tinker Sly uses this cry in the Induction of the Shrew when telling others to hush.

clue.text: Three of us lost our wickets? But the creases are now rectified

definitions.note: a sentence describing the result; the answer is the verb phrase for smoothing creases

blocks.note: three people named in a row: I, Ron and Ed
in cricket a batsman who loses his wicket is out

explanation.surface: Three batsmen are dismissed, but the crease is now put right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creases' looks like the cricket batting line, which fits the wickets; here it means wrinkles in cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrinkles in fabric that have been pressed flat with a hot iron are smoothed away and corrected.

clue.text: Lo thy ego is some study!

indicators.note: 'that's some study!' exclaims at something remarkably made, hinting the letters are worked into something new

blocks.note: the eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A mock-archaic exclamation that someone's own self is quite a subject for study.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethology is the scientific study of animal behaviour, a field of research and so a study.

clue.text: Where's Susan?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone asking the whereabouts of a woman called Susan
setter's reading: the English actress whose surname is also a southern county

explanation.walkthrough: Susan Hampshire was a British actress, famous in 1970 for the television serial The Forsyte Saga.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a county on England's south coast, and also the surname that follows the actress Susan.

clue.text: A member is O so forgetful!

indicators.note: the clue claims the answer with the letter attached is the forgetful state, so that letter must come away

blocks.note: limbo is a state of neglect and oblivion, being forgotten
taken as written, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone in a society is so absent-minded, oh dear!
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as 'a member plus O is the forgotten state': LIMB with O is LIMBO.
explanation.definitionFit: An arm or leg is a limb, and anatomy calls such parts of the body its members.

clue.text: Mowgli's fraternisation with them got Baloo's monkey up

definitions.text: Mowgli's fraternisation with them got Baloo's monkey up

blocks.note: surface reading: the jungle boy making friends with some group
setter's reading: the bear was angered, and the group in question is literally the monkey tribe

explanation.surface: The bear Baloo was furious that the jungle boy Mowgli mixed with a certain crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's Jungle Book the Monkey-People kidnap Mowgli after he plays with them; 'get one's monkey up' means to anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's name for the lawless Monkey-People, whom Baloo forbids Mowgli to associate with in the jungle.

clue.text: Stony? At least you've bread and butter

definitions.note: an adjective hinting at the noun: the stone step at a front door

blocks.note: first meaning: the stone step outside a house door, and where the stony broke end up
second meaning: a thick hunk cut from a loaf and buttered

explanation.surface: Even if you are stony broke, at least you still have bread and butter.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a very thick slice of bread is called by the same word as the front step.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the flat stone at a house entrance and a chunky slice of buttered bread.

clue.text: Where we are dying to go?

definitions.text: Where we are dying to go?

blocks.clueFragment: Where we are dying to go
blocks.note: surface reading: a place we are eager to visit
setter's reading: to 'go west' is slang for to die

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dying to go' sounds like eagerness; literally, those who die are said to go west.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a formal word for the West, the direction slang links with death.

clue.text: Father has the minutes

blocks.note: surface reading: Dad is keeping the record of a meeting
setter's reading: the old man with the scythe and hourglass, whose stuff is measured in minutes

explanation.surface: Dad is holding the written record of the committee meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Time personifies the passage of hours, and minutes are the units it is counted in.

clue.text: The Captain didn't give a damn, he said

definitions.text: The Captain didn't give a damn, he said

blocks.clueFragment: The Captain didn't give a damn
blocks.note: surface reading: a careless ship's master
setter's reading: the Pinafore captain sings that he never uses a big, big D, meaning he never swears

explanation.surface: A ship's captain claimed he simply did not care.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, Captain Corcoran boasts he never says 'damme' ('What, never?' 'Hardly ever!').
explanation.definitionFit: Corcoran is the surname of the commanding officer of HMS Pinafore in the comic opera.

clue.text: Total tax fare goes up, but he's harmonious to a degree.

definitions.note: a person: a holder of a music degree

indicators.note: in a down entry rising upward means reading from the bottom, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: a taxi, the vehicle whose fare you pay
a total is a sum

explanation.surface: The overall tax on a fare rises, but someone stays calm about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Mus.Bac. abbreviates Bachelor of Music; 'harmonious to a degree' means musical, by degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bachelor of Music holds a university qualification in music, harmony being part of that study.

clue.text: Engine part that was controversial in Lilliput

blocks.note: first meaning: the larger end of a connecting rod, round the crankshaft
second meaning: in Gulliver's Travels the Lilliputians warred over which end of an egg to break

explanation.surface: A component of an engine that caused an argument among the tiny people of Lilliput.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift satirised religious schism with the Big-Endians and Little-Endians.
explanation.definitionFit: In motor engineering it names the crank end of a connecting rod, and in Swift the rounder egg end.

clue.text: Work is a habit with her

definitions.text: Work is a habit with her

blocks.clueFragment: Work is a habit with her
blocks.note: surface reading: a workaholic woman for whom labour is routine
setter's reading: a habit is a garment, which this maker produces

explanation.surface: A woman for whom working has become an ingrained routine.
explanation.definitionFit: This tradesperson makes or supplies outfits for the stage, and a habit is a type of garment.

clue.text: Rebellious Jack gets a letter, joins up

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: one who joins up

blocks.note: Jack Cade led a rebellion against Henry VI in 1450
one letter of the alphabet, here T

explanation.surface: A rebel called Jack receives a letter and enlists.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade is in Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 2; 'a letter' is unusually open here, leaving the solver to pick T.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a young recruit training for military service, someone who has enlisted.

clue.text: Partitioned area of a certain diagram

indicators.note: 'of' marks the answer as a part taken out of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the word break

explanation.surface: A region of a particular chart is divided off by lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partitioned area' sounds like a box on a diagram; it is the country split in 1947.
explanation.definitionFit: British India was divided into two independent states, India and Pakistan, at independence in 1947.

clue.text: Heavens, a duenna? Law, a severe one!

blocks.note: first meaning: the constellation of the Dragon, a fierce chaperone being a dragon
second meaning: the Athenian lawgiver whose code was notoriously harsh

explanation.surface: Exclamations of shock at a strict chaperone and a harsh lawgiver.
explanation.walkthrough: A duenna is a stern older woman guarding a girl, and such a guardian is called a dragon; 'Heavens' places it in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco is both the Dragon constellation in the night sky and the lawmaker behind the term draconian.

clue.text: On with the ball, though liquor flow grudgingly!

blocks.note: first meaning: to move forward with a football under close control
second meaning: to trickle out in drops

explanation.surface: Let the party go on, though the drink is running out slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' suggests a dance and 'liquor' the bar; it is football and a trickle.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers advancing a ball with small touches and liquid running in a slow trickle.

clue.text: It's hard at the end, being on foot

definitions.text: It's hard at the end, being on foot

blocks.clueFragment: It's hard at the end, being on foot
blocks.note: surface reading: a long walk becomes tough by the finish
setter's reading: a hard covering at the tip of a digit of the foot

explanation.surface: Travelling on foot is hardest in the last stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: The horny plate covering the tip of each toe is the hard part at the end of a toe.

clue.text: Among the ice-creams he's "dying for a cuppa!"

indicators.note: 'among' says the answer sits inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the word break

explanation.surface: At the ice-cream stall, one person craves a cup of tea instead.
explanation.walkthrough: A cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A theic is someone addicted to tea, a person always craving another cup.

clue.text: A union that leaves us open-mouthed

definitions.text: A union that leaves us open-mouthed

blocks.clueFragment: A union that leaves us open-mouthed
blocks.note: surface reading: a marriage or trade union that astonishes us
setter's reading: a joining of two vowel sounds, said with the mouth open

explanation.surface: A marriage or alliance so surprising that we gape at it.
explanation.definitionFit: In phonetics this is a gliding blend of two vowel sounds in one syllable, as in 'coin'.
